**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Leadership team  
**Re:** Regulatory strategy for AI pneumothorax triage software for chest X-ray (US and EU)

### 1. Bottom line
- **US:** Position the product as **computer-aided triage and notification (CADt)** and file a **510(k)** under 21 CFR 892.2080 (Class II). Pneumothorax triage tools are already cleared (e.g., GE Healthcare's Critical Care Suite), so predicates exist. Start with a **Pre-Submission** and include a **Predetermined Change Control Plan (PCCP)**.
- **EU:** Under MDR Rule 11 this is at least **Class IIa**. Plan for **IIb**, because a missed or delayed pneumothorax can cause serious deterioration. You need a Notified Body (NB), and the product is a **high-risk AI system** under the EU AI Act.
- **Sequencing:** Build one QMS and one evidence package that cover both regimes. FDA clearance will probably come first. Open the NB application at the same time, because NB queues are the longest step.

### 2. Intended use drives everything
Recommended draft:
> Software that analyzes adult chest radiographs and notifies radiologists of cases with suspected pneumothorax to help prioritize the worklist. It does not mark or annotate images, remove cases from the standard reading queue, or replace the radiologist's full review.

Leave these out of v1:
- On-image localization. It moves you to CADe (892.2070), which comes with heavier reader-study expectations.
- "Diagnoses" or "rules out" language.
- Autonomous reporting.
- Pediatric use without pediatric data.

Treat them as later expansions.

### 3. US pathway
- **Classification:** 892.2080, product code QFM or QAS (confirm against your chosen predicate). Special controls require:
  - standalone performance data
  - labeling that explains the triage-only role
  - "not for diagnostic use" on any preview image
- **Pivotal evidence:**
  - Retrospective standalone study on an independent, multi-site US dataset never used for training or tuning. Ground truth comes from 2–3 board-certified radiologists with adjudication.
  - Sensitivity and specificity with 95% CIs (precedents generally show lower bounds above 80%), AUC, and time-to-notification versus standard of care.
  - Subgroups: age, sex, race/ethnicity, site, equipment manufacturer, AP vs PA, portable/ICU studies, pneumothorax size, and **chest tubes** (a classic shortcut-learning confounder). Include look-alikes such as skin folds and bullae.
- **Software and AI documentation:** Follow FDA's device software functions guidance (likely Basic documentation level; confirm at Pre-Sub). Also follow its AI-enabled device software guidance on data management, model description, bias analysis and performance monitoring.
- **Cybersecurity:** The product is a "cyber device" under FD&C Act §524B, so you need an SBOM, a threat model and a vulnerability management plan.
- **QMS:** Comply with the QMSR, which aligns with ISO 13485 and took effect in February 2026.
- **PCCP:** Pre-specify retraining triggers, data sources, acceptance criteria and rollback, so model updates don't need new 510(k)s.

### 4. EU pathway
- **Classification:** Document your Rule 11 rationale using MDCG 2019-11. Expect NBs to push toward IIb for chest X-ray triage.
- **Conformity assessment:** Annex IX (QMS audit plus technical documentation per Annexes II/III). Also:
  - appoint a PRRC
  - appoint an EU Authorised Representative if you are based outside the EU
  - register in EUDAMED
  - assign UDI
- **Clinical evaluation (MDCG 2020-1):** Cover valid clinical association, technical performance and clinical performance. Reuse the US study, but add **European data** from different populations, equipment and workflows. Plan PMCF as real-world performance monitoring.
- **PMS:** PMS plan, PSUR (annual for IIb, every two years for IIa), vigilance.
- **AI Act:** Because it is an MDR device that needs NB assessment, it is high-risk under Art. 6(1). The obligations cover data governance, logging, transparency, human oversight, accuracy and robustness. They currently apply from August 2027, but the EU's Digital Omnibus package would defer them, possibly to 2028, so confirm the current date. Build them into the MDR technical file now, since your NB is expected to assess both.
- **Changes:** MDR has no PCCP equivalent, so significant changes need NB approval. Documenting predefined change boundaries supports the AI Act's Art. 43(4) "pre-determined changes" provision and simplifies change notifications.
- **Data protection:** Establish a GDPR legal basis and complete a DPIA for EU training and validation data.

### 5. Shared standards
- ISO 13485.
- ISO 14971, including automation bias, missed alerts and alert fatigue.
- IEC 62304, likely Class B.
- IEC 62366-1, with summative usability testing with radiologists.
- IEC 81001-5-1 for security.
- Verification of DICOM/PACS/RIS integration.

### 6. Indicative timeline
| Month | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 0–2 | Intended use and classification rationale locked; Pre-Sub filed; NB contracted |
| 2–6 | Pivotal study, usability, V&V, cybersecurity testing |
| 6–7 | 510(k) submitted (90 FDA review days; plan for 5–7 months to decision) |
| 7–9 | MDR technical documentation submitted |
| 12–20 | CE certificate (depends on the NB) |

### 7. Key risks
1. **Claim creep from sales or marketing:** keep a controlled claims list and have regulatory review all materials.
2. **NB capacity:** contract early and hold a pre-application meeting.
3. **Bias or generalizability findings:** lock diverse, multi-vendor test sets before the model is frozen.
4. **Post-market drift:** monitor against defined thresholds and actions.
5. **IIa vs IIb dispute:** prepare IIb-grade evidence from the start, because rework costs more.

### 8. Decisions needed
- Confirm a triage-only scope for v1.
- Approve the budget for pivotal data acquisition and NB fees.
- Confirm the legal manufacturer entity and whether an EU Authorised Representative is needed.

*Verify product codes, predicates and current guidance with regulatory counsel before filing.*

# Software Development Plan: Outline
**Product:** [Name], standalone SaMD | **Software safety class:** B per IEC 62304:2006+A1:2015 | **Doc ID / Revision / Approvals:** [ ]

*Clause references appear in brackets, so the plan also works as a compliance map.*

## 1. Purpose and scope
- Why the plan exists.
- Software systems, components and versions covered.
- Exclusions, e.g., non-device modules and IT infrastructure.
- Relationship to QMS procedures (ISO 13485) and to system-level design controls [5.1.3].

## 2. References and definitions
- Standards: IEC 62304, ISO 14971, ISO 13485, IEC 62366-1, IEC 82304-1, IEC 81001-5-1.
- Regulatory: FDA device software premarket guidance; EU MDR Annex I §17.
- Internal SOPs the plan relies on.
- Glossary.

## 3. System description and safety classification [4.3]
- Intended use, high-level architecture, and operating environment (cloud, OS, browsers, interfaces).
- **Class B rationale:** after crediting external (non-software) risk controls, the worst credible hazardous situation from a software failure is non-serious injury. Cross-reference the ISO 14971 hazard analysis.
- Any software items classified differently, with the segregation rationale.
- Legacy software, if any [4.4].

## 4. Organization and responsibilities
- Roles: software lead, developers, test/QA, risk manager, configuration manager, regulatory, clinical and independent reviewers.
- Competence and training requirements.
- Who reviews and approves each deliverable.

## 5. Lifecycle model [5.1.1]
- The model chosen (e.g., agile per AAMI TIR45) and how 62304 activities map onto sprints, increments and releases.
- Design reviews, phase gates, and a definition of done that includes documentation.
- **Deliverables table:** activity, output, owner, reviewer, approver.

## 6. Development activities
- **Requirements analysis [5.2]:**
  - Inputs: system requirements, risk controls, usability, security, data/interfaces and regulatory requirements.
  - Requirement attributes and review criteria.
  - Re-evaluating risk when requirements change.
- **Architectural design [5.3]:**
  - Decomposition into software items, and their interfaces.
  - SOUP functional/performance requirements and the hardware/software each SOUP item needs [5.3.3–5.3.4].
  - Architecture verification.
- **Detailed design [5.4.1]:** Refine the architecture into software units. Detailed unit design [5.4.2–5.4.4] is required only for Class C, so state whether you will do it anyway.
- **Unit implementation and verification [5.5]:** methods (code review, static analysis, unit tests), acceptance criteria [5.5.3] and coverage targets.
- **Integration and integration testing [5.6]:** integration order, environment, regression strategy.
- **System testing [5.7]:** protocols traced to requirements, test environment, anomaly handling, retest rules.
- **Release [5.8]:** release criteria, evaluation of known residual anomalies, release notes, archiving, reproducible builds.

## 7. Integration and verification planning [5.1.5, 5.1.6]
- Verification tasks, milestones, methods and acceptance criteria for each deliverable.
- Reviewer independence.
- Traceability across requirements, architecture, tests and risk controls, including the tool and format used.

## 8. Software risk management [5.1.7, 7]
- Link to the ISO 14971 risk management plan.
- Software items that contribute to hazardous situations, including SOUP failures and review of SOUP anomaly lists [7.1].
- Defining, implementing and verifying risk control measures [7.2–7.3].
- Risk assessment of changes [7.4].

## 9. SOUP management
- SOUP inventory: name, version, supplier, purpose.
- Selection criteria.
- Review of published anomaly lists.
- Monitoring for updates and vulnerabilities.
- SBOM.

## 10. Avoiding common software defects [5.1.12]
- Defect categories relevant to your tech stack (e.g., CWE Top 25, OWASP).
- Coding standards and static analysis, and how CI enforces them.

## 11. Documentation planning [5.1.8]
- Document list with purpose, owner, format, review/approval and change control for each.

## 12. Configuration management [5.1.9–5.1.11, 8]
- Configuration items: code, SOUP, build scripts, documents, test assets, and ML models/datasets if applicable.
- Supporting items to control [5.1.10]: compilers, IDEs, CI/CD and test tools, plus how tools are validated.
- Items placed under control before verification [5.1.11].
- Branching, versioning, baselines, change requests and change records.

## 13. Problem resolution [9]
- Problem report contents and criticality rating.
- Investigation and link to change control.
- Trend analysis and verification of fixes.
- Interfaces with complaint handling and CAPA.

## 14. Maintenance [6]
- Reference the software maintenance plan, which covers:
  - feedback intake
  - post-market SOUP and vulnerability monitoring
  - patch criteria

## 15. Interfaces with other processes
- Usability (IEC 62366-1).
- Cybersecurity (IEC 81001-5-1).
- Clinical/performance validation.
- Regulatory submissions.

## 16. Plan maintenance [5.1.2]
- Triggers for updating the plan.
- Revision history.

## Appendices
- **A.** Class B compliance matrix (clause → SDP section → evidence record).
- **B.** Deliverables and approvals.
- **C.** Tool list with validation status.

---

### Practical notes
- **Not required for Class B:**
  - 5.1.4 (standards, methods and tools planning)
  - 5.3.5 (segregation for risk control)
  - 5.4.2–5.4.4 (detailed unit design)
  - 5.5.4 (additional unit acceptance criteria)

  Many teams still include tools planning because auditors ask about it.
- **Keep it lean:** Reference SOPs instead of copying them. Use this plan for project-specific decisions.
- **Edition check:** Most regulators currently recognize 62304:2006+A1:2015. A new edition is in development and changes the classification approach, so confirm which version your target markets expect.
